catalog_quote: This study focusses on the stress system of the Northern dialect. Hess (1977:404) writes that the major stress in Northern Lushootseed words occurs on the first non-schwa of a stem, or, if all the vowels are schwas, on the first schwa. Hess also mentions that there seems to be a "sub-classs of lexical suffixes which receive primary stress regardless of preceding vowels." Yet, as we see in (1), there is significant variation in the placement of stress in Lushootseed and it can occur in every available (stressable) position. ... From my data it appears that stress assignment in Lushootseed is not predictable in about ten to fifteen percent of cases. [p.127] ... We can define strong roots as those with the shape CVCX, which attract stress to the expected leftmost position of a word. audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Bianco 1995 PDF/txt at the stated printed pages (127, 128, 129). (2) The deciding source is a short 1995 conference working paper formalising Hess 1977's descriptive rule; better descriptions exist (Kye 2023 UW dissertation, Urbanczyk 1996). I fetched sources Kye 2023 (open access) to; its sec.10.2.2 (pp.227-233) states at most one stress per word, Northern dialect stress on the first non-schwa (full-vowel) syllable of the stem, schwa roots cede stress to a full-vowel lexical suffix, with word-specific and dialect-specific exceptions, and no established secondary stress. This confirms the catalog's weight-hedged coding (full-vs-reduced vowel weight, unbounded leftmost, lexical exceptions ~10-15%). One refinement worth carrying into the record's caution field: the r

sources.citation: Kye, Ted Kyoungsirk. 2023. A Grammar of Lushootseed: Phonetics, Phonology, Morphology. PhD dissertation, University of Washington (ResearchWorks handle 1773/51196, Open Access; 432 pp.).
sources.quote: p.227: 'In Lushootseed, there is at most one stressed syllable per word. Roots that are monosyllabic tend to be the location of primary stress in a word.' p.227-228: 'According to Hess (1977), there are dialectal differences ... in the Northern dialect, the location of primary stress is on the first non-schwa syllable of a stem' (kʷəd-ˈad N vs ˈkʷəd-əd S; dəˈč̓uʔ N vs ˈdəč̓uʔ S); Southern 'stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable' (Hess 1977). p.229: lexical suffix with a full vowel is stressed when the root has schwa (dəˈgʷ-ič), root keeps stress when it has a full vowel (ˈx̌ʷil-ič),
